## Newton iteration in the reaction extents (`phase_equilibrate_tp`) {#sec-ch05-newton}

### Summary

The solver applies Newton's method to the residuals of @sec-ch05-conditions, with the reaction extents as unknowns.
Each iteration builds the exact Jacobian of the residuals with respect to the extents and takes the bounded Newton step
of @sec-ch10-newton, which keeps every amount above `mole-floor`. The step is then halved until the largest residual
decreases. It stops when the largest residual is below the target, or reports why it could not
(@sec-ch05-diagnostics). One cell is solved per thread, on the CPU or on CUDA, and every cell of a batch is
independent.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Solve @eq-ch05-conditions-residual for the extents, @eq-ch05-newton-jacobian.

**Data.** Amounts in and out [mol]; $T$, $p$ and $\ln K^\circ_r$ per cell; gain and diagnostics out.

**Placement.** `EquilibriumTP` forward, per cell, on CPU or CUDA.

**Activation.** Always; YAML `max-iter` (50), `mole-floor` ($10^{-30}$).

**Guarantee / limits.** Amounts stay above the floor and elements are conserved; convergence is not guaranteed.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Symbols as in @sec-ch05-conditions. Local symbols: $\mathsf J$, the Jacobian of the residuals with respect to the
extents [mol$^{-1}$]; $\boldsymbol\delta$, the Newton direction in extents [mol]; $\lambda$, the step scale [-];
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{floor}}$, the value of `mole-floor` [mol]; $\nu_{\pi r} = \sum_{n:\,\pi(n)=\pi} \nu_{nr}$, the
change of phase $\pi$'s total per unit extent of reaction $r$ [-].

### Derivation

With $\boldsymbol{\mathcal N} = \boldsymbol{\mathcal N}^0 + \mathsf S\boldsymbol\xi$, a change of extent $\xi_k$
changes $\mathcal N_n$ by $\nu_{nk}$ and the phase total $\mathcal N_\pi$ by $\nu_{\pi k}$. The pressure factor of the
gas activities is constant. Differentiating @eq-ch05-conditions-residual:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \ln a_n}{\partial \xi_k} &= \frac{\nu_{nk}}{\mathcal N_n} - \frac{\nu_{\pi(n) k}}{\mathcal N_{\pi(n)}} , \\
\mathsf J_{rk} = \frac{\partial r_r}{\partial \xi_k}
  &= \sum_n \nu_{nr} \Big( \frac{\nu_{nk}}{\mathcal N_n} - \frac{\nu_{\pi(n) k}}{\mathcal N_{\pi(n)}} \Big) .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-newton-jacobian}

`phase_equilibrate_tp` ({{< code src/equilibrium/phase_equilibrate_tp.h phase_equilibrate_tp >}}) builds
`phase_stoich` ($\nu_{\pi k}$) once and then `jac[j * nreaction + k]` exactly as in @eq-ch05-newton-jacobian.
`check_ch5_equilibrium.py` line d checks the code itself. On the three-phase system of `newton_check.py`, with
`max-iter: 1`, the gain kintera returns (the Jacobian at the input) equals @eq-ch05-newton-jacobian to 0.0 relative
difference.[^ch05-newton-check] That system is a deliberately singular example. It has three phases and two
elements, so by the phase rule of @sec-ch05-conditions its Jacobian is singular in exact arithmetic (line f: smallest
singular value $1.6\times10^{-17}$ at the start state on x86_64, $2.5\times10^{-16}$ on arm64). The solve on it is therefore ill-posed, and which status it
ends with is decided by rounding. An exactly zero LU pivot sends the step to the least-squares fallback, and status 3
follows only if that fallback fails too (with `max-iter: 1` it has a single inner iteration). A tiny non-zero pivot
gives a huge direct step that no scale accepts (status 4). On the build of the run record it is status 3 with
`max-iter: 1` and status 4 after one step with the default. A clean arm64 build of the pin gives status 4 with
`max-iter: 1`, as does the PyPI 2.6.4 wheel, whose equilibrium code is the same. The gain is formed before the step, so the comparison of line d holds either way. `newton_check.py` is a numpy transcription of the code's formula, not a call to the
built solver. Its line `[C1]` checks that the formula is the derivative of the residual (central differences, on the
same system), and `[C3]` shows that a one-species phase contributes nothing, because its activity is 1 whatever its
amount. The Newton direction
solves $\mathsf J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf r$. The amounts after a step of scale $\lambda$ must stay above the floor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal N_n + \lambda \sum_k \nu_{nk}\,\delta_k &> \mathcal N_{\mathrm{floor}} \quad \text{for every } n , \\
-\sum_k \nu_{nk}\,\delta_k &\le \mathcal N_n - \mathcal N_{\mathrm{floor}} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch05-newton-bounds}

The second line, at $\lambda = 1$, is the constraint form $\mathsf C\boldsymbol\delta \le \mathbf d$ of
@sec-ch10-newton, with $\mathsf C = -\mathsf S$ and $\mathbf d = \boldsymbol{\mathcal N} - \mathcal N_{\mathrm{floor}}$.
The code sets these rows as `constraints` and `bounds`. In this solver they never change the direction. The slack
$\mathbf d$ is strictly positive in every state the iteration sees: the input passes the status-1 test
$\mathcal N_n > \mathcal N_{\mathrm{floor}}$, every accepted trial passes the same test, and in floating point
$x > f$ implies $x - f > 0$ (with gradual underflow; with flush-to-zero it still holds for the default floor
$10^{-30}$, whose spacing is a normal number in double and single precision). `constrained_newton_step` leaves the direct direction only for a bound with no slack, or
when the LU solve fails (an exactly zero pivot) or returns non-finite values. So here the least-squares fallback runs
only in the last case. The floor acts in the line search instead (Numerical method, step 6).

**Why a direct solve.** `constrained_newton_step` factorises $\mathsf J$ itself rather than forming the normal
equations $\mathsf J^{\mathsf T}\mathsf J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathsf J^{\mathsf T}\mathbf r$. The singular values of
$\mathsf J^{\mathsf T}\mathsf J$ are the squares of those of $\mathsf J$, so the normal equations would square the
condition number. The direct LU solve loses digits in proportion to $\operatorname{cond}(\mathsf J)$ only, which is
the same argument as for the direct form of the constrained least-squares step (@sec-ch04-active-set).

**What the line search guarantees.** Along the Newton direction, a step of scale $\lambda$ changes the residuals by

$$
\mathbf r(\boldsymbol{\mathcal N} + \lambda\mathsf S\boldsymbol\delta) = \mathbf r + \lambda\,\mathsf J\boldsymbol\delta
  + O(\lambda^2) = (1 - \lambda)\,\mathbf r + O(\lambda^2) ,
$$

so every non-zero residual shrinks in proportion, and $\max_r|r_r|$ falls for every small enough $\lambda$. Every
amount is above the floor before the step, so small steps also keep the amounts above it. In exact arithmetic the
halving loop therefore accepts a step whenever the direction is the Newton direction, provided the decrease sets in
above the smallest scale, $10^{-12}$, and the trial stays above the floor at that scale. A phase that should vanish
breaks the second condition. The Newton step drives its amount below the floor, and the floor test rejects every
scale down to $10^{-12}$, so the loop ends with status 4 (@sec-ch05-diagnostics). The merit function is the largest
residual, and any decrease is accepted. A sufficient-decrease (Armijo) test would not change this case, because the
step is cut by the floor, not by a weak decrease.[^ch05-newton-refs] `check_ch5_equilibrium.py` line e reproduces
kintera with a numpy copy of the iteration that has a plain LU direction and no least-squares fallback. For a
converged start and for a start whose liquid must vanish, the status, step count and error are the same, and the
amounts agree to round-off: 0.0 on the build of the run record, and $5\times10^{-21}$ mol on an arm64 build of the
pin. The line therefore tests the amounts to round-off, not bitwise: to $10^{-14}$ of the largest amount, and each
amount to $10^{-5}$ of itself. The second test is needed because the first, $10^{-14}$ mol here, is larger than the
returned liquid of $3.03\times10^{-15}$ mol and alone would not resolve it.

### Numerical method

`phase_equilibrate_tp` ({{< code src/equilibrium/phase_equilibrate_tp.h phase_equilibrate_tp >}}) runs these steps in
each cell:

1. **Input checks.** A non-positive temperature or pressure, an empty species, reaction or phase list, a gas phase index out
   of range, or any input amount not above `mole-floor` returns status 1 at once, with the input copied to the output.
2. **Target.** The stop test is $\max_r |r_r| \le \max(\ln(1 + \texttt{ftol}), 4\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}})$; see
   @sec-ch05-diagnostics.
3. **Residuals.** Evaluate @eq-ch05-conditions-residual (@sec-ch05-conditions). If the target is met, stop with
   status 0.
4. **Jacobian.** Build @eq-ch05-newton-jacobian at the current amounts.
5. **Direction.** Call `constrained_newton_step` ({{< code src/math/constrained_newton.h constrained_newton_step >}})
   with the rows of @eq-ch05-newton-bounds. It solves $\mathsf J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf r$ directly and keeps that
   direction unless it leaves a bound with no slack, and only then solves the constrained least-squares problem
   (@sec-ch10-newton, @sec-ch10-kkt), with regularisation $10^{-12}$ and at most `max-iter` inner iterations. A
   failure there stops the solve with status 3. Every slack is positive here (Derivation), so the fallback runs only
   when the LU solve fails or returns non-finite values.
6. **Line search.** Try $\lambda = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots$ down to $10^{-12}$. A trial is formed by
   `constrained_newton_trial` ({{< code src/math/constrained_newton.h constrained_newton_trial >}}) and accepted when
   every amount is finite and above the floor and the largest residual is smaller than before. If no scale is
   accepted, the solve stops with status 4.
7. **Repeat** from step 3, up to `max-iter` iterations; reaching the cap gives status 2.

The amounts change only by $\mathsf S\lambda\boldsymbol\delta$, so the elements are conserved to round-off
(@eq-ch05-conditions-extent). The per-cell scratch arrays come from a memory pool: on CUDA the driver sizes it with
`equilibrium_space`, including the workspace of the least-squares fallback
(`call_equilibrium_cuda`, {{< code src/equilibrium/equilibrium_dispatch.cu call_equilibrium_cuda >}}). On the CPU the
cells are split over threads by `call_equilibrium_cpu`
({{< code src/equilibrium/equilibrium_dispatch.cpp call_equilibrium_cpu >}}). @fig-ch05-newton-loop gives the order
of the steps.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch05-newton-loop
#| fig-cap: "One iteration of the log-K solver. Boxes are the steps in order; the green arrow repeats an accepted step up to max-iter; grey notes give the status each exit sets."
#| fig-alt: "Four boxes left to right: residuals and stop test, Jacobian in reaction extents, bounded Newton step, halve until the error falls; an arrow loops from the last box back to the first."
#| echo: false
from kintera_report.ch05.figures.fig_newton_loop import make_fig
make_fig()
```

On a hot H-O gas of six species and four reactions, solved from 2 H$_2$ + O$_2$ with traces of the others at 15
temperatures between 1500 and 5000 K, every solve converges in 11 to 14 iterations. The largest reported error is
$2.0\times10^{-9}$, and H and O are conserved to $4.4\times10^{-16}$ relative. The same runs on CUDA take the same
iteration counts and agree with the CPU to $1.1\times10^{-16}$ in mole fraction.[^ch05-ho-run]

: Code map of the Newton iteration. {#tbl-ch05-newton-code}

`EquilibriumTPImpl::forward` broadcasts $T$, $p$, the amounts and $\ln K^\circ_r$ against each other, so one set of
constants can serve many cells or each cell can have its own. Inputs must share a device and a floating type. The
`warm_start` argument is accepted and ignored.

### Tests

| test (ctest name) | what it asserts | tolerance | where the tolerance comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_equilibrium.py` (`test_ill_conditioned_multiphase_newton_step`) | an ill-conditioned three-phase state converges, with every amount positive | error $< 10^{-8}$ | the `ftol` of the case |
| `test_equilibrium.release` (`IdealGasReaction`) | the solve converges on CPU and CUDA, in float and double | error $< 10^{-5}$ | not stated in the test |

: Tests of the Newton iteration. {#tbl-ch05-newton-tests}

The docstring of `test_ill_conditioned_multiphase_newton_step` describes it as a regression for precision loss in
the normal equations, which the direct solve of step 5 avoids; which path each of its iterations takes is not
recorded by the test (hypothesis: the direct one). Both tests pass on both builds (@sec-ch05-conditions,
Tests). No test makes the line search or the least-squares fallback run, and no test checks element conservation on
a multiphase case.

### Limits

- **Convergence is not guaranteed.** The line search only asks that the largest residual decrease; a cell can stop
  with status 4 for reasons other than a vanishing phase. How often that happens on hard systems is not measured.
- **At most 64 components** (`EquilibriumOptionsImpl::validate`), and the reactions must be linearly independent
  (@sec-ch05-options). Independent reactions still give a singular Jacobian when there are more phases than independent elements
  (the phase rule, @sec-ch05-conditions); the rank check does not detect it, and such a solve ends with status 3 or 4
  depending on rounding.
- **A species cannot reach zero.** The floor test of the line search rejects every step that would take a species
  below `mole-floor`. A species that should vanish stays just above the floor, and the cell ends with status 4
  (@sec-ch05-diagnostics).
